message.reasoning:
I need to decide whether to sell houses or hotels on my properties, or declare bankruptcy.

I have $61 cash but owe $550. I can sell hotels on ST_CHARLES_PLACE, STATES_AVENUE, and VIRGINIA_AVENUE. I cannot mortgage any properties. I am calculating how much cash I would get from selling those hotels.

Selling a hotel on a pink property returns about $50. Selling all four houses returns $200. That gives roughly $250 total from one property.

Selling one hotel and its four houses returns $250, bringing total cash to $311. That still leaves a $239 shortfall. Selling two full strips returns $500, giving $561 total and covering the $550 rent with $11 remaining.

The engine allows multiple liquidation rounds. I can sell a hotel and receive its value, then sell the four houses in a separate turn if needed.

Selling all three hotels returns $150. That brings total cash to $211, leaving a $339 shortfall. I still need to sell houses.

Standard Monopoly rules require selling houses evenly across a monopoly. I cannot strip one property completely while others retain hotels. I must sell hotels from all three properties before I can sell any houses.

The engine will reject any sell plan that breaks even building rules. I cannot strip one property while leaving hotels on the others.

Selling one hotel from each property raises cash to $211. Then selling two houses on each property adds $300, bringing total cash to $511. That leaves a $39 shortfall.

Selling three houses on each property adds $450, bringing total cash to $661. That covers the $550 rent and leaves a surplus of $111, with one house remaining on every property.

The engine applies one sell action at a time and asks again if the shortfall remains. I must therefore liquidate in legal even stages.

I am also checking whether selling a hotel on only one property would break even-building rules if the other two properties still have hotels.

Standard Monopoly rules allow selling a hotel from one property while others retain hotels. A hotel equals five houses, so converting it to four houses creates only a one-level difference. The even-building rule permits at most one house gap between properties in a color group. I can therefore sell hotels individually without stripping all three properties first.

I am weighing whether to sell all three hotels at once or strip them down one by one. I want to minimize building loss while still raising the $489 needed to cover the rent. I am also reconsidering whether bankruptcy might be preferable.

I need to sell ten $50 units to raise the $489 shortfall. I am now weighing how downgrading my hotels will affect future rent income, since St. Charles Place and States Avenue currently yield $750 each while Virginia Avenue yields $900. I am also checking the board order to see where player one will land next.

Player one is on Mediterranean Avenue. A roll of six lands on St. Charles Place, eight on States Avenue, and nine on Virginia Avenue. That means they have a roughly 39 percent chance of hitting a pink property next turn.

I realize that keeping hotels intact is my only viable win path. If player one lands on a pink property while I still have hotels, they would pay $750 to $900 and likely be forced to sell dark blues. I must therefore liquidate the minimum amount needed to cover the $550 rent, which requires selling ten $50 units for $500. I am now calculating how to do this while preserving as much pink development as possible.

Selling three hotels and seven houses is the exact minimum to cover the rent. That yields $500 in sales, bringing total cash to $561. One property ends with one house, two with two houses each. I am now checking the rent values for those two-house configurations.

Two houses on each pink property yield only $150 to $180 in rent. Player one has $957 cash, so they can easily pay that amount. After paying the $550 rent, I would have just $11 left and weak rent income. This leaves me vulnerable because player one will likely land on a pink property next turn.

I realized that selling two hotels completely while keeping one hotel intact would violate even-building rules. The gap between a property at level zero and one still at level five exceeds the permitted one-level difference. I must therefore sell all three hotels evenly.

Mortgaging the pinks would require selling all buildings first, so it is not viable. The minimum liquidation should leave two houses on Virginia Avenue and one house each on St. Charles Place and States Avenue.

I cannot sell houses on a property that still has a hotel, because the engine requires the property to have houses before it can sell them. I must therefore sell the hotels first, then sell the houses in a separate turn.

I will sell all three hotels in a single plan. That raises cash to $211 and leaves a $339 shortfall, but it is the most efficient way to liquidate while staying even. The engine accepts multiple items in one sell_plan.

I will sell one hotel from each of the three properties in this turn. I will not try to sell houses in the same action, because the engine would reject it while hotels still remain. I am now deciding which property should keep only one house.

St. Charles Place will keep one house. States Avenue and Virginia Avenue will each keep two houses. Bankruptcy is not an option because the other players are already bankrupt. The $550 rent on Vermont Avenue is correct.

I confirmed that selling a hotel returns only $50 and converts it to four houses. The engine schema separates HOTEL and HOUSE actions, so I cannot sell the entire property at once. The bank has enough houses available.

messages.content:
You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.
